examples.claim: Existing systems waste 60%–80% of memory through fragmentation and over-reservation
examples.source: Blog: 'existing systems waste 60% – 80% of memory due to fragmentation and over-reservation'.

examples.claim: One block for all vectors vs separate blocks/tables per head and layer showed no performance difference; authors chose the latter for easy implementation
examples.source: Paper §4.1: 'The two designs have no performance difference and we choose the second one for easy implementation.'

examples.claim: ShareGPT best with block sizes 16–128; Alpaca fine at 16 and 32, worse above; default block size 16
examples.source: Paper §7.2: 'In the ShareGPT trace, block sizes from 16 to 128 lead to the best performance. In the Alpaca trace, while the block size 16 and 32 work well...'; 'vLLM sets its default block size as 16'.

examples.claim: --block-size: contiguous cache block size in tokens; None means default; always int after construction
examples.source: Engine args: 'Size of a contiguous cache block in number of tokens. Accepts None (meaning "use default"). After construction, always int.'

examples.claim: A GPU warp is assigned per block for coalesced access; block copies are batched in one kernel instead of many cudaMemcpyAsync calls
examples.source: Paper §5.1: 'we assign a GPU warp to read each block'; 'Fused block copy ... batch the copy operations for different blocks into a single kernel launch'.

examples.claim: The block engine allocates one contiguous chunk of GPU DRAM split into physical blocks, also on CPU RAM for swapping; block tables keep #filled
examples.source: Paper §4.2: 'a block engine allocates a contiguous chunk of GPU DRAM and divides it into physical KV blocks (this is also done on CPU RAM for swapping)'; '#filled positions'.

examples.claim: 7-token prompt, 4 tokens per block: 0→7 (#filled 4), 1→1 (3); after first decode 1→1 (4); second decode allocates 2→3
examples.source: Paper §4.3 / Fig. 6 walk-through: physical blocks 7 and 1, one slot left, then new physical block 3.

examples.claim: B=16, 700-token prompt, three outputs: 44 blocks (43 full, last 12 tokens), 132 blocks without sharing vs 46 with sharing; two copies
examples.source: Writer's labelled example ('가상의 숫자'); arithmetic checked: ceil(700/16)=44, 700-43*16=12, 3*44=132, 43+3=46; refcount 3 -> 2 copies, third writes in place per paper's CoW rule.

examples.claim: Beam k=4: blocks 2, 4, 5, 8 freed; 9–12 allocated; all share 0, 1, 3; candidates 0,1 share 6 and 2,3 share 7
examples.source: Paper §4.4: 'vLLM frees all physical blocks whose reference counts reach 0 (blocks 2, 4, 5, 8). Then, vLLM allocates new physical blocks (blocks 9-12)...'

examples.claim: --scheduling-policy fcfs (default) or priority; lower value first, arrival time breaks ties
examples.source: Engine args: '"priority" means requests are handled based on given priority (lower value means earlier handling) and time of arrival deciding any ties). Default: fcfs'; parsed.

examples.claim: v0.8.1: V1 needs no KV swapping for preemption and drops GPU↔CPU swapping, best_of and per-request logits processors
examples.source: v0.8.1 V1 user guide: 'V1 no longer requires KV cache swapping to handle request preemptions'; best_of, Per-Request Logits Processors, GPU<>CPU KV Cache Swapping all '🔴 Deprecated'.

examples.claim: Linux and Python 3.11–3.14; no native Windows (WSL or forks); NVIDIA compute capability 7.5+ (T4, A100, L4, H100, B200)
examples.source: GPU install page Requirements: 'Python: 3.11 -- 3.14', 'vLLM does not support Windows natively', 'compute capability 7.5 or higher (e.g., T4, RTX20xx, A100, L4, H100, B200, etc.)'.

examples.claim: nm-vllm 0.5.0 docs say the number of KV cache blocks depends on --gpu-memory-utilization
examples.source: nm-vllm 0.5.0 engine_args has only the fraction definition (default 0.9) and --num-gpu-blocks-override; no block-count statement.

examples.claim: VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE is GiB; default 0 means it does not override the size; TP rank weight shard + space over one NUMA node -> exitcode 9; legacy, use --kv-cache-memory-bytes
examples.source: CPU page supports GiB, exitcode 9 and 'legacy setting; use --kv-cache-memory-bytes'; it says only 'Default value is 0' — the 'does not override' meaning is not stated (envs.py: unset -> None, '4 GB').

examples.claim: Introl cites vLLM 793 tok/s vs Ollama 41 tok/s, P99 80 ms vs 673 ms
examples.source: Introl: 'vLLM achieves throughput of 793 tokens per second compared to Ollama's 41 tokens per second at equivalent configurations, with P99 latency of 80ms versus 673ms.'

off_sample_findings.claim: A 'third-party post introducing V1' reports hash-based prefix caching with LRU in V0 and V1 and <1% throughput loss at 0% hit rate
off_sample_findings.source: The source is the official vLLM blog 'vLLM V1: A Major Upgrade to vLLM's Core Architecture' (2025-01-27, vLLM team): 'vLLM V1, like V0, uses hash-based prefix caching and LRU-based cache eviction ... less than 1% decrease in throughput even when the cache hit rate is 0%'. Numbers right, attribution wrong.

off_sample_findings.claim: The 55% memory saving is what the 3-parallel-completion HF/TGI benchmark numbers measure
off_sample_findings.source: Blog: 'cutting their memory usage by up to 55%. This can translate into up to 2.2x improvement in throughput.' The 8.5–15x / 3.3–3.5x figures compare whole systems; the blog does not attribute them to sharing.

off_sample_findings.claim: The 60–80% waste comes exactly from this kind of reservation
off_sample_findings.source: Blog: 'waste 60% – 80% of memory due to fragmentation and over-reservation'; paper adds external fragmentation and missed sharing. The sentence narrows the cause to reservation.

off_sample_findings.claim: Against current serving engines, take the paper's 2–4x as the realistic starting point
off_sample_findings.source: Paper: 2–4x vs FasterTransformer and Orca (2022-2023 systems). No source compares vLLM with current engines; this is the writer's extrapolation presented as guidance.

off_sample_findings.claim: If the preemption counter keeps rising, lower --max-num-seqs, add KV capacity or add instances
off_sample_findings.source: runpod 'vLLM Explained': 'If ... vllm:num_preemptions_total grows steadily under nominal load, you need to reduce --max-model-len, raise --gpu-memory-utilization, or add capacity'; --max-num-seqs is not named.

off_sample_findings.claim: A steadily rising preemption counter means the batch cap is high relative to KV cache capacity
off_sample_findings.source: No source states this cause; runpod calls sustained preemption a degradation state and lists other remedies.

off_sample_findings.claim: Swapping back can take hundreds of ms
off_sample_findings.source: runpod: 'On a PCIe 4.0 x16 link (~32 GB/s), restoring a long-context sequence on Llama-3-70B can take hundreds of milliseconds'; the post drops model, link and context scope (L225, L229).
Docker docs: 'You can either use the ipc=host flag or --shm-size flag'; the post's next sentence says the same, so the first sentence overstates.
